blocks.text: 3. Expectation and variance of random variables

segments.text: The expectation (mean) and variance of a random variable generalise the descriptive-statistics concepts of Chapter 1 to a theoretical probability distribution rather than an observed dataset — computed as a probability-weighted sum (discrete) or integral (continuous) rather than a simple average over collected data, but interpreted identically as a measure of central tendency and spread respectively.

blocks.text: 4. Important distributions: binomial, Poisson, and normal

items.text: : models the number of successes in a fixed number (n) of independent trials, each with the same success probability (p) — applicable whenever an experiment consists of repeated identical yes/no trials (mean = np, variance = np(1−p)).

: models the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, when events happen independently at a constant average rate (λ) — often used as an approximation to the binomial when n is large and p is small (rare events over many trials), with mean and variance both equal to λ.

segments.text: Under specific conditions, one distribution can be used to approximate another where exact calculation would be cumbersome — the Poisson approximation to the binomial (above), and the normal approximation to the binomial (valid when np and n(1−p) are both sufficiently large, since the binomial distribution’s shape becomes increasingly bell-like as n grows) are the two most commonly applied approximations at this syllabus level. Correctly identifying which named distribution actually fits a given real-world scenario’s assumptions — rather than defaulting to whichever formula is most familiar — is the central applied skill this chapter tests.

items.text: Discrete variables use a probability mass function and sums; continuous variables use a probability density function and integrals, with the CDF applying uniformly to both.
Expectation and variance of a random variable are the theoretical, probability-weighted analogues of the sample mean and variance from descriptive statistics.

The binomial (fixed trials, success/failure), Poisson (rate-based event counts), and normal (continuous, bell-shaped) distributions are the three most important named distributions, each with specific defining assumptions.
The Poisson can approximate the binomial for rare events over many trials; the normal can approximate the binomial when both np and n(1−p) are sufficiently large.
Correctly matching a real scenario’s assumptions to the appropriate distribution — not just applying a familiar formula — is the essential applied skill.
